appraisal_events.evidence: ils hébergeaient — avec la parfaite innocence d'honnêtes hôteliers qui ont chez eux, sans le savoir, un célèbre brigand — un des membres les plus élégants du Jockey-Club, ami préféré du comte de Paris et du prince de Galles, un des hommes les plus choyés de la haute société du faubourg Saint-Germain.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator sharply elevates Swann by revealing that behind his modest, familiar bourgeois appearance he is in fact one of the most brilliant and sought-after figures of the highest aristocratic society, a truth his own hosts never suspect.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Êtes-vous seulement connaisseur ? [...] vous devez vous faire repasser des croûtes par les marchands » [...] « On peut dire que vous êtes un vrai type, monsieur Swann ! » [...] « Oui, chez une princesse du demi-monde ! » avait répondu ma tante en haussant les épaules [...] avec une ironie sereine.
appraisal_events.explanation: The grand'tante repeatedly mocks and doubts Swann's taste, treats him as a comic figure, and dismisses his real high-society connections as a joke, locally diminishing him within the family's own judgment even though the narrator's framing shows this scorn to be based on ignorance.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's true standing is revealed to be at the pinnacle of fashionable aristocratic society, far above what his provincial hosts imagine, sharply elevating him in the reader's eyes.
Within the family's own local treatment, the grand'tante persistently mocks and belittles Swann, denying him credibility as a connoisseur and treating his real social eminence as a punchline.
The narrator explicitly frames her mockery of Swann as evidence that she is 'the only somewhat vulgar person in our family,' locally diminishing her even as she disparages him.

ambiguities: The grand'tante's disparaging remarks about Swann are explicitly framed by the narrator as revealing her own vulgarity ('la seule personne un peu vulgaire de notre famille'), so E2 should be read as ironized rather than an endorsed evaluation of Swann.

'ma grand’tante' does not match any entry on the reference sheet (she is distinct from tante Léonie, who is bedridden and does not travel or receive guests in Paris), so her identity is left unresolved.
